posts.image_prompt: Towering curved dry-stone granite walls of an ancient African enclosure, neatly stacked stones without mortar, a conical stone tower inside, savanna grass and msasa trees, golden hour light, wide cinematic shot
posts.caption:
🏰 THE STONE CITY THEY SAID AFRICANS COULDN'T BUILD

In southern Africa stand the ruins of Great Zimbabwe — a city built and rebuilt between roughly the 11th and 15th centuries.

Its Great Enclosure has walls about 11 metres high and around 250 metres long. Every stone was stacked by hand. No mortar holds them together.

Archaeologists have found Chinese porcelain and Persian glass there, proof that this inland city was tied into Indian Ocean trade.

Yet when European explorer Karl Mauch saw the ruins in 1871, he refused to believe local people built them and linked them to King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Later colonial authorities pushed the same idea.

The evidence says otherwise. Archaeologists concluded the city was built by the ancestors of the Shona people. In 1980, the newly independent nation named itself after it: Zimbabwe.

Why do you think the truth was resisted for so long?

posts.topic: Rongorongo, the script of Easter Island
posts.title: The island that invented writing — and lost it

scenes.image_prompt: A dark wooden tablet covered in rows of tiny carved bird and human-like symbols, lit by a single beam of light in a museum vault
scenes.narration: On a remote Pacific island, people carved a script no one can read today.

scenes.image_prompt: Moai statues on a grassy Easter Island hillside under a dramatic Pacific sky, waves in the distance, cinematic
scenes.narration: It's called rongorongo, from Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island. The first outsider to report it was a missionary, in eighteen sixty-four.

scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of hands turning an ancient carved wooden tablet upside down, rows of small engraved symbols, warm candlelight
scenes.narration: The signs run in alternating lines. After each line, the reader turns the tablet upside down to continue.

scenes.image_prompt: An empty Polynesian coastal village at dusk, abandoned canoes on the beach, somber mood, nineteenth century
scenes.narration: But in the eighteen sixties, slave raids and epidemics devastated the island. The people who could read the tablets were lost.

scenes.image_prompt: A scientist in a modern laboratory examining a tiny wood sample beside an ancient carved tablet, soft blue light
scenes.narration: Fewer than thirty objects survive, scattered in museums. In twenty twenty-four, researchers dated the wood of one tablet to around the year fifteen hundred, long before Europeans arrived.

scenes.image_prompt: A carved wooden tablet resting on volcanic rock at sunset, the ocean glowing behind it
scenes.narration: So did Rapa Nui invent writing on its own? Tell us what you think, and follow for more.

posts.caption:
🗿 A script no one alive can read.

Rongorongo was carved on wooden tablets on Rapa Nui (Easter Island). Fewer than 30 objects survive, and the script remains undeciphered. A 2024 study dated the wood of one tablet to around 1493–1509 — centuries before European contact.

Independent invention of writing? Share your view 👇

posts.image_prompt: A glamorous 1940s Hollywood actress in an elegant dress sitting at a drafting table at night, sketching mechanical diagrams, warm lamp light, film-noir atmosphere, no text
posts.caption:
🎬 THE MOVIE STAR WHO PATENTED A SECRET SIGNAL

In the 1940s, Hedy Lamarr was one of Hollywood's most famous faces. Few people knew she was also an inventor.

During World War II she worked with composer George Antheil on a way to stop radio-controlled torpedoes from being jammed: make the signal hop between multiple frequencies, so an enemy couldn't lock onto it.

On August 11, 1942, they received U.S. Patent No. 2,292,387 for a 'Secret Communication System'. The National Inventors Council showed little interest at the time.

Years later, the idea surfaced in military communications — including on U.S. ships during the 1962 blockade of Cuba. Frequency hopping is now seen as an important step in wireless communication.

In 1997 the Electronic Frontier Foundation honoured her work, and in 2014 she was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame.

Who's another inventor history forgot to credit?

posts.topic: The whaleship Essex, the real Moby-Dick
posts.title: The whale that sank a ship
posts.hook_text: A WHALE RAMMED THIS SHIP. TWICE.

scenes.image_prompt: A colossal sperm whale surging out of dark Pacific water toward the bow of a wooden 19th-century whaling ship, spray everywhere
scenes.narration: In 1820, a whale rammed a ship twice, and sank it.

scenes.image_prompt: A weathered wooden whaling ship with patched sails on a calm blue Pacific ocean, crew in small rowing boats nearby, 1820
scenes.narration: The Essex sailed from Nantucket with twenty-one men. On November 20, 1820, deep in the Pacific, a huge sperm whale rammed her.
scenes.label: NANTUCKET

scenes.image_prompt: Below-deck view of a ship's hull splintering inward, seawater rushing in, lanterns swinging, sailors scrambling
scenes.narration: Then it came back and hit her again. The ship went down. The crew escaped in three small whaleboats.

scenes.image_prompt: Three tiny open wooden boats adrift on an endless empty ocean under a blazing sun, gaunt sailors in ragged shirts
scenes.narration: Far from any land, they chose a long route toward South America.

scenes.image_prompt: A lone rescue ship with full sails approaching a battered small boat on a grey sea, distant figures waving
scenes.narration: About three months later, rescue ships found the boats. Only eight men survived the ordeal.
scenes.label: 8 SURVIVORS

scenes.image_prompt: A 19th-century writer at a candlelit desk reading an old printed shipwreck narrative, sea charts and a quill nearby
scenes.narration: First mate Owen Chase wrote it all down. Years later, a writer named Herman Melville read his account.

scenes.image_prompt: A blue cloth-bound book with a gold embossed whale on the cover resting on a ship's wooden deck, sea mist
scenes.narration: Here's the twist. On October 18, 1851, Melville's novel came out in London under a different title: The Whale. Today we call it Moby-Dick.

scenes.image_prompt: A huge sperm whale's tail rising above a stormy sea at dusk, no ships in sight
scenes.narration: Would you ever go back to sea after that? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🐋 ON THIS DAY in 1851, Moby-Dick was first published — in London, under the title "The Whale".

Melville drew on a true disaster. In 1820, a sperm whale rammed the Nantucket whaleship Essex twice and sank her in the middle of the Pacific. Her crew drifted for months in open boats; only eight men survived.

First mate Owen Chase's account of the wreck became one of Melville's key inspirations.

Would you have taken the longer route to safety, or risked the unknown islands? 👇

📅 ON THIS DAY in 1867, one flag came down in Sitka — and the U.S. grew by nearly 600,000 square miles.

On October 18, 1867, about 250 American soldiers marched up Castle Hill in Sitka, the capital of Russian America. At around 3:30 p.m., the Russian flag was lowered and the Stars and Stripes went up in its place.

The price: $7.2 million — less than 2 cents an acre. Secretary of State William Seward had agreed the deal with Russian minister Eduard de Stoeckl that March.

The strange part? For the Russians watching, it wasn't October 18 at all. Russia still used the old Julian calendar, 12 days behind, so their date was October 6.

Critics mocked the deal as "Seward's Folly" and "Seward's Icebox" — until the Klondike gold strike of 1896 changed most minds.

The cancelled check, dated August 1, 1868, still survives in the U.S. National Archives.

What do you think is the greatest bargain in history?

posts.title: Titanic's Last 160 Minutes: Seven Warnings, 20 Lifeboats and a Silent Radio
posts.hook_text: SEVEN WARNINGS. TWENTY LIFEBOATS. ONE NIGHT.

scenes.narration: At 11:39 p.m. on April 14, 1912, lookout Frederick Fleet saw a dark shape in front of the Titanic. He called the bridge: iceberg, right ahead.
A minute later, the largest ship in the world scraped along the ice. Less than three hours after that, she was gone, and around 1,500 people were dead.
In the next few minutes you'll hear about the seven ice warnings, the lifeboats that left half empty, and the nearby ship whose radio had just gone silent.
Titanic was built by Harland and Wolff in Belfast for the White Star Line, side by side with her near-identical sister ship, the Olympic.
scenes.label: BELFAST

scenes.narration: She was almost 883 feet long, with ten decks and a gross tonnage of over 46,000. Passengers and crew together, she was built to carry more than 3,300 people.
On April 10, 1912, she left Southampton on her maiden voyage to New York, with roughly 2,200 passengers and crew on board.
scenes.label: 10 APR 1912

scenes.narration: In command was Captain Edward Smith. He was 62 years old, with about forty years at sea and twenty-seven years as a captain.
The first ice warning reached Titanic at nine in the morning on April 14, from the liner Caronia. By that night, her wireless operators had received seven.
Even so, the ship kept up a speed of about 22 knots — faster than her normal service speed of 21, and close to her top speed.
The nearest ship, the Californian, had warned of ice too. At 11:30 p.m., her only radio operator, Cyril Evans, switched off his set and went to bed.
Ten minutes later, Titanic struck. The ice opened at least five of her sixteen watertight compartments. She could stay afloat with four flooded — not five.
Her chief designer, Thomas Andrews, was travelling on board. He worked out what the flooding meant, and concluded that the ship was doomed.
At 12:45 a.m., the first distress call went out, using the old code CQD, later the new SOS. That same minute, lifeboat number 7 was lowered.
It had room for 65 people. Only about 28 were in it. Titanic carried just 20 lifeboats, with space for about 1,178 people, out of more than 2,200 on board.
Survivors remembered the ship's band playing lively tunes, even ragtime, as the boats were loaded. Whether they ended with the hymn Nearer, My God, to Thee is still disputed.
Around 2:15 a.m. the bow plunged and the stern rose high into the air. The ship broke apart, and by 2:20 a.m. Titanic had disappeared.
Hundreds were left in water around minus two degrees Celsius. Most of the roughly 1,500 who died were killed by the cold.
Fifty-eight miles away, the Cunard liner Carpathia picked up the distress call and raced towards Titanic's last reported position.
scenes.label: 58 MILES

scenes.narration: At 4:10 a.m., Carpathia picked up the first lifeboat. By morning she had rescued every survivor — about 710 people, most of them women and children.
On April 18, Carpathia docked in New York. Crowds and reporters were waiting, and the disaster was already front-page news around the world.
scenes.label: 18 APR 1912

scenes.narration: Inquiries in America and Britain followed. They led to a new treaty in 1914: the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, which still exists today.
For 73 years, nobody knew exactly where she lay. Then, on September 1, 1985, a joint French and American expedition found the wreck, about two and a half miles down.
scenes.label: 1 SEP 1985

scenes.narration: On the sea floor, the wreck showed what some survivors had described from the lifeboats: Titanic had broken apart before she went under.
Seven warnings. Twenty lifeboats. A nearby ship with its radio switched off. Which one change do you think would have saved the most lives? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🚢 Seven ice warnings. Twenty lifeboats. A nearby ship whose radio had just been switched off.

This is the minute-by-minute story of Titanic's last 160 minutes — from Frederick Fleet's call of "Iceberg, right ahead!" at 11:39 p.m. to the moment she vanished at 2:20 a.m. on April 15, 1912.

You'll see why a lifeboat built for 65 left with about 28 people, why the closest ship never answered, and what the wreck revealed when it was finally found in 1985.

Which single change would have saved the most lives that night?
